b: zahra hasanaat was founded in mumbai in 1996 on a simple principle: enquire about the wellbeing of others — do not wait for them to come to you; go to them, ask how they are, and be helpful in their time of need. three decades on, that principle has grown into an integrated model of community development. we work alongside families facing poverty, hunger, educational inequity, poor access lasting change possible. guiding principles the ultimate aim of everything zahra hasanaat does is not only to provide aid but to help individuals and families achieve self reliance. upliftment, not charity, benefits both givers and receivers: it builds connectedness, capability and dignity. we interact with every person with respect and compassion, ensuring the dignity of those receiving help is maintained. enrolment in our programs is deliberately light touch — no one should have to prove desperation to receive support. the organisation is committed to good governance, transparency, fair management, responsible use of funds, and accountability. a governing board oversees stewardship, approvals and systems, supported by dedicated teams for fundraising, communications, and financial budgets and audits. how we work the centre model each zahra hasanaat centre is a grassroots hub — a welcoming public space where people access services, build relationships and gain skills, shaped by its own neighbourhood and shared across a growing network. centres begin with one or two strong entry points, such as meals or tuition, and grow into fuller community platforms over time. seven connected verticals nutrition, medical care, education, livelihoods, wellness, community outreach and cross community collaboration are designed to reinforce one another, so a family is supported through connected channels rather than fragmented service lines. people as infrastructure counsellors, outreach workers and more than 100 volunteers are the human system through which trust and continuity are built — treated as essential, never peripheral.

s: Safe, joyful learning spaces where children and adults grow in language, creativity and confidence.
x: Our Education programme exists to close the gap between the education children receive and the education they deserve. It creates spaces — physical and relational — where children from underserved families can grow in language, creativity and confidence. Built
b: our education programme exists to close the gap between the education children receive and the education they deserve. it creates spaces — physical and relational — where children from underserved families can grow in language, creativity and confidence. built on years of tuition classes and scholarship support for more than 100 students, the programme now spans a community library, english language learning, creative expression workshops, vocational training for women and computer literacy classes. what we do community library a free multilingual library of around 2,000 books in marathi, hindi and english, with informal floor seating designed for children and space for up to 50 readers. reading circles and storytelling sessions nurture a culture of reading for joy, and children use the space for independent self study before and after classes. english language learning structured, child centred english sessions that offer an experiential alternative to rote instruction, drawing on waldorf education principles. the first cohort completed 18 session days with 88 per cent average attendance, and an adapted curriculum for adult learners is in development. creative expression workshops regular workshops in art, dance and theatre give children a joyful outlet for self expression and confidence building, co facilitated by teachers, librarians and volunteers. vocational training for women stitching and mehndi classes teach practical, income generating skills, with flexible scheduling designed around the household responsibilities many women carry. computer literacy foundational digital skills classes for young people and adults, using the computer stations at the centre. tuition and scholarship support long running tuition classes and scholarship support that have reached more than 100 students. our approach we start from the belief that learning is transformative only when it is safe, joyful and deeply human. sessions are experiential and child centred rather than rote based, organised in short modular units so that children facing unstable home circumstances can keep participating, and supported by home visits and family engagement that build the trust which brings learners through the door. teachers track attendance, language progress and confidence over time, and children who need wider help are connected to counselling, health and nutrition support through our other programmes. particular care goes into removing barriers to participation for girls and women. at a glance more than 100 students have received tuition classes and scholarship support the community library holds around 2,000 books in marathi, hindi and english, with space for up to 50 readers the first english language learning cohort completed 18 session days with an average attendance of 88 per cent nine children in grades 5–8 completed phase 1 of the english language learning programme the programme received its first institutional education grant, a seed grant from the circle india (teach for india)

s: Needs-based grants and interest-free loans that help families move from crisis to stability to self-reliance.
x: Poverty is not a fixed condition — it is a circumstance that can change when people are met with genuine support, not charity alone. Our Grants, Loans & Livelihoods programme provides needs assessed grants and interest free loans, guided by careful assessment
b: poverty is not a fixed condition — it is a circumstance that can change when people are met with genuine support, not charity alone. our grants, loans & livelihoods programme provides needs assessed grants and interest free loans, guided by careful assessment and an ongoing relationship with each family. the goal is not dependency but movement: from crisis towards stability, and from stability towards self reliance. what we do community grants needs assessed grants for medical emergencies, medicines, school fees, food rations and household essentials, and significant life events — including support for widows, debt restructuring and home improvement. urgent cases are fast tracked so help arrives when it is needed. interest free loans small loans for business capital, goods and house purchase, disbursed entirely without interest. repayments are reinvested into new loans, building a revolving fund that allows the programme to sustain itself and reach more families over time. assessment and case management every family receives a comprehensive assessment by a counsellor or social worker — including home visits — before any aid decision. each family is then assigned a named case worker who reviews their progress on a six month cycle, so support is a continuing relationship rather than a one time transaction. livelihoods and economic empowerment grant and loan recipients are connected to our wider programmes — education, health, nutrition and vocational training — so that financial support is one thread in a family's larger journey towards independence. a fair, structured process applications come through a central intake office and an online application portal, with every case documented and every decision recorded. support levels are structured and consistent, so assistance is allocated fairly and reaches the families who genuinely need it most. our approach assessment comes before assistance: a counsellor or social worker visits and assesses every family before any aid is disbursed, because home visits consistently surface needs that an application form alone cannot show. each family then has a single named point of contact who stays with them through six month review cycles, which we have found builds trust and encourages families to take up complementary support such as counselling, education and vocational training. loans carry no interest, and repayments seed new loans — so the programme is designed to become self sustaining rather than dependent on continuous fundraising. at a glance 39 individuals supported through community grants in the last 12 months 5 active loan cases, spanning business capital, goods support and house purchase every family receives a comprehensive counsellor or social worker assessment before any aid decision families are reviewed by their assigned case worker on a six month cycle all loans are interest free

b: food is often where a family's relationship with zahra hasanaat begins. since 2018 our kitchens have served more than 698,000 meals — over 850 every day — alongside structured ration support that eases pressure on household budgets between cycles. we are building this work into a single, dignified food support system that brings together cooked meals, grocery support, home delivery and community giving. what we do daily cooked meals our kitchens prepare and serve more than 850 hot meals every day, on site and through outreach distribution — immediate hunger relief offered in a spirit of welcome. household ration support registered households receive a grocery package every two months, built around staples such as rice, wheat flour, dal, oil, sugar, salt and tea, with a limited choice of add ons so families take home what they will actually use. home delivery for elders, people with disabilities, those who are unwell and anyone facing barriers to travel, delivery is a normal part of the service rather than an exception. simple enrolment and scheduling families can join through a referral, an outreach visit or a simple whatsapp message. intake asks only for the basics, and collection times are confirmed by message — no long queues, and no need to repeat personal hardship at every visit. volunteer and in kind giving volunteers run packing days, delivery routes and intake follow up, while donation drives gather staples and hygiene items — including seasonal and festival food baskets that have run for the past three years. nutrition quality with guidance from volunteer medical and public health advisers, we are shaping food baskets towards better dietary balance, with child and women sensitive items where possible and practical household guidance on healthier everyday meals. our approach the programme is designed so that no one has to prove desperation in order to eat. enrolment is light touch, collection works by appointment rather than queue, packaging is neat and discreet, and home delivery is standard for those who cannot travel. this matters because many vulnerable families are excluded from formal ration systems by documentation gaps or administrative barriers — a community programme should close that gap, not repeat it. food support also serves as a doorway, connecting families to education, health and livelihood support across our other programmes. at a glance more than 850 cooked meals served daily over 698,000 meals served since 2018 household grocery support provided on a two month cycle seasonal and festival food baskets distributed for the past three years

s: Bringing specialist healthcare, preventive care and continuity of care to underserved families in rural and semi-urban India.
x: The medical programme brings quality, dignified healthcare to underserved families — especially children — in rural and semi urban India. Health is rarely a standalone need: it is bound up with a family's nutrition, income and access to education. By meeting m
b: the medical programme brings quality, dignified healthcare to underserved families — especially children — in rural and semi urban india. health is rarely a standalone need: it is bound up with a family's nutrition, income and access to education. by meeting medical needs with genuine care and continuity, the programme builds trusted relationships with communities and opens a pathway towards wider family support. what we do paediatric surgery camps specialist camps bring paediatric surgery, ophthalmology, orthopaedics, neurology, neuro rehabilitation and speech therapy to rural communities in a single setting. children who need surgery are identified at camp and their treatment is facilitated at partner hospitals, followed by post operative care. mother and child health camps camps with obstetric, gynaecological and paediatric specialists provide consultations and necessary medications, with counsellors following up on each family's treatment plan. outpatient services a standing outpatient partnership extends access to consultations between camps, giving families a reliable point of care throughout the year. preventive health and telemedicine telemedicine consultations and subsidised testing packages reach people who cannot travel for in person care, supporting prevention and early detection for high risk groups. referrals and follow up a referral network connects families to partner hospitals for secondary and specialist care, with structured follow up — surgical, rehabilitative and psychosocial — so no one is left to navigate recovery alone. our approach the programme follows a continuity model: identification at camp, facilitation of treatment, surgery or specialist care at a partner hospital, and structured post operative follow up. hospital partnerships — including white lotus international hospital, mgm hospital and wockhardt — make specialist paediatric care accessible at a fraction of its usual cost, and often where it is not otherwise available. every medical touchpoint is paired with counsellor support, connecting healthcare to nutrition, education and livelihood assistance, so that a single consultation can become the start of holistic support for the whole family. at a glance 120 people attended the inaugural paediatric surgery and neuro rehabilitation camp in raigad district (february 2026) 46 children seen and over 60 specialist consultations completed at the inaugural camp 8 children identified for surgery — all successfully treated at partner hospitals 5 referral cases connected to appropriate specialist centres 9 children placed on medical management plans 11 children scheduled for six month follow up reviews 50 families received consultations and medications at the mother and child health camp, each with counsellor follow up six paediatric subspecialties brought together in a single camp: surgery, ophthalmology, orthopaedics, neurology, neuro rehabilitation and speech therapy

s: Building trust in underserved neighbourhoods through art, listening and long-term family support.
x: Community Outreach is the connective tissue of Zahra Hasanaat's work — how trust is built before services are offered, and how families are seen before they are helped. Rather than arriving with aid or assessment forms, our teams lead with art and listening, r
b: community outreach is the connective tissue of zahra hasanaat's work — how trust is built before services are offered, and how families are seen before they are helped. rather than arriving with aid or assessment forms, our teams lead with art and listening, returning month after month to the same neighbourhoods so that deeper support becomes possible. the programme works through three strands: neighbourhood outreach visits, a dedicated counsellor team, and a supervised volunteer network. what we do neighbourhood art visits monthly visits of around an hour and a half to underserved neighbourhoods (bastis), built around a participatory art activity — build our dream community, using cloth, chalk or paper — that brings children, adults and community workers together. each visit opens with an icebreaker and closes with shared reflection. home visits for families who have engaged with the programme or asked for deeper support, team members make individual home visits to understand each household's circumstances more fully and prepare tailored support proposals. counsellor led family follow up a dedicated counsellor team keeps in regular, proactive contact with every family in the organisation's network — asking after their wellbeing rather than waiting to be asked. a structured monthly follow up tracks family welfare, children's schooling and health, and progress towards goals set with each household. connecting families to wider support when a need is identified, the team prepares a support proposal that is reviewed by counsellor leads before any assistance is arranged, with monthly follow up afterwards. outreach links families into the organisation's nutrition, medical, education and financial programmes, and assistance is connected to positive steps such as school attendance and health check ups. volunteer training and participation every volunteer completes a training workshop covering deep listening, role clarity and ethical boundaries before joining fieldwork. volunteers support neighbourhood visits, ration distribution, storytelling sessions at the community library, and medical and education camps. safeguarding and accountability all volunteers and social workers sign a formal agreement covering scope of work, safeguarding, child protection and confidentiality, and work within a clear reporting structure from family to volunteer to coordinator to organisation. our approach the model is deliberately phased: it begins with open community visits led by art and listening, moves to individual home visits as trust grows, and only then designs tailored support — in recognition that lasting upliftment is only possible when families trust the people who come to help them. a counsellor team maintains each relationship over time through structured monthly follow up, so that no family falls through the cracks. trained, supervised volunteers provide the consistent human presence that makes this possible, and every touchpoint can connect a family to nutrition, medical, education or livelihoods support. at a glance monthly neighbourhood visits of approximately 1.5 hours each active outreach in four neighbourhood areas: konkipada, sainath nagar, rabodi and bhimanagar programme launched with an inaugural volunteer training workshop on 18 february 2026 a 3.5 hour training workshop for all outreach volunteers and team members before fieldwork structured monthly welfare follow up in place for all families in contact signed agreements covering safeguarding, child protection and confidentiality for all volunteers and social workers

(click here to watch this video which summarizes the events “glimpse of the taqreeb conference.”) taqreeb was a vision of syedna khuzaima qutbuddin: to bring people of all faiths together, to work towards common humanitarian goals, to achieve the full potential of religion as a force for good in this world that we all inhabit. today, his son and successor, syedna taher fakhruddin saheb, the 54th dai l mutlaq, has put that vision into action by launching the taqreeb conference series. the conference brought together eminent scholars, activists, religious leaders from over 20 cities internationally. the first day included panels on, 1) plurality in religious thought, 2) entangled histories, imagined politics, 3) leadership and peace. the second day included a 1) special session with religious leaders, 2) engaging precedents for peace in the present, 3) race, caste, & identity in contemporary india, 4) contemporary politics & visions for the future. on the second day syedna taher fakhruddin saheb head of the dawoodi bohra community presented the syedna qutbuddin harmony prize to the dalai lama, religious leader of the tibetans. the prize is awarded annually to honour an individual or organisation whose work has had an exceptional impact in promoting harmony and peace in india as well as globally. the prize carries a monetary value of rs10 lac. present at this gathering were senior religious leaders of all the major religions of india, meeting in the convention hall of jawaharlal nehru university: his holiness acharya dr. lokesh muni, jain leader, his eminence archbishop anil joseph thomas couto, archbishop of the delhi diocese of the catholic church, sardar manjit singh gk, president of delhi sikh gurdwara management committee, rabbi ezekiel isaac malekar, head of the jewish community in new delhi, shri gairgopal das of iskon, dr. ali k. merchant, and justice aziz k. ahmadi, former chief justice of india. syedna fakhruddin, in his address, invited all the leaders to discuss and implement a coalition to fight the forces of conflict and division in india and the world. click here to watch syedna fakhruddin’s address (12 mins). the dalai lama expressed sincere appreciation to syedna taher fakhruddin tus, as a muslim leader for organizing a conference that brought together different faiths (click here to watch the dalai lama’s address). he expressed sadness for the sectarian divisions that were dividing the country and congratulated syedna for leading the country in a more positive direction. he said that the modern study of psychology pales in comparison to india’s deep and age old tradition psychological awareness. he said, “to decrease destructive emotions like fear we must increase positive emotions like love”. jain leader acharya lokesh muni said that syedna fakhruddin saheb and his predecessors, by their work on the ground across india in providing institutions of civil society such as schools and hospitals, has brought the concept of harmony into action. click here to view media reports of the conference. we are hopeful that with our combined efforts the ripples of this conference will carry not only across the country but also across the world. further details and proceedings from the conference will be published in due course.

b: the 2nd taqreeb conference entitled ideas of harmonious coexistence: religions and philosophies of india took place at jawaharlal nehru university, december 27 28 2017. view glimpses of the taqreeb conference taqreeb was a vision of syedna khuzaima qutbuddin: to bring people of all faiths together, to work towards common humanitarian goals, to achieve the full potential of religion as a force for good in this world that we all inhabit. today, his son and successor, syedna taher fakhruddin saheb, the 54th dai l mutlaq, has put that vision into action by launching the taqreeb conference series. the conference brought together eminent scholars, activists, religious leaders from over 20 cities internationally. the first day included panels on, 1) plurality in religious thought, 2) entangled histories, imagined politics, 3) leadership and peace. the second day included a 1) special session with religious leaders, 2) engaging precedents for peace in the present, 3) race, caste, & identity in contemporary india, 4) contemporary politics & visions for the future. on the second day syedna taher fakhruddin saheb presented the syedna qutbuddin harmony prize to the dalai lama, religious leader of the tibetans. the prize is awarded annually to honour an individual or organisation whose work has had an exceptional impact in promoting harmony and peace in india as well as globally. the prize carries a monetary value of rs 10 lac. present at this gathering were senior religious leaders of all the major religions of india, meeting in the convention hall of jawaharlal nehru university: his holiness acharya dr. lokesh muni, jain leader, his eminence archbishop anil joseph thomas couto, archbishop of the delhi diocese of the catholic church, sardar manjit singh gk, president of delhi sikh gurdwara management committee, rabbi ezekiel isaac malekar, head of the jewish community in new delhi, shri gairgopal das of iskon, dr. ali k. merchant, and justice aziz k. ahmadi, former chief justice of india. syedna fakhruddin, in his address, invited all the leaders to discuss and implement a coalition to fight the forces of conflict and division in india and the world. watch syedna taher fakhruddin tus' address to the conference the dalai lama expressed sincere appreciation to syedna taher fakhruddin tus, as a muslim leader for organizing a conference that brought together different faiths. he expressed sadness for the sectarian divisions that were dividing the country and congratulated syedna for leading the country in a more positive direction. he said that the modern study of psychology pales in comparison to india’s deep and age old tradition psychological awareness. he said, “to decrease destructive emotions like fear we must increase positive emotions like love”. watch his holiness the dalai lama's address to the conference jain leader acharya lokesh muni said that syedna fakhruddin saheb and his predecessors, by their work on the ground across india in providing institutions of civil society such as schools and hospitals, has brought the concept of harmony into action.

b: gastroesophageal reflux disease (gerd) is common condition, especially among people over the age of 40 years. there are are many different ways that gerd can present. heartburn is one common typical presentation of gerd. there can be many other symptoms as well. in some countries, 20% to 30% of patients between the ages of 40 and 64 complain of symptoms of gerd to their doctors. this prevalence is likely to be an underestimate as many people do not consult a physician. gerd affects many aspects of everyday life including work, sleep, and enjoyment of food. there a many lifestyle factors that can cause and worsen symptoms of gerd. there can also be serious consequences, if gerd is not addressed or treated. a clear understanding of basic anatomy and function of the gastrointestinal tract is important for the prevention and management of reflux disease. the zahra hasanaat health initiative aims to promote good health in our community. the mission is to educate, webinar entitled “gastroesophageal reflux disease: a burning issue” was delivered by dr. fehmida chipty on 12mi raat of ramadaan (saturday, 27th june) at 9.30pm ist (12:00pm est – noon). participants had an opportunity to ask questions to dr. chipty towards the end of the talk. dr. chipty is a board certified gastroenterologist practicing in the greater boston area since 1997. she is a graduate of wellesley college and the university of massachusetts medical school.she completed her internal medicine residency and subspecialty training in gastroenterology at the albert einstein college of medicine/ montefiore medical center. dr. chipty believes in the central role of the physician as an educator. she practices with the goal of helping patients understand their medical conditions in order empower them to participate in their health improvement.
